title: why so many gods?
hookLine: a sage is asked how many gods there are and counts down from 3,306 to one

lines: HOW MANY GODS DO YOU HAVE?
cards: Someone at school or work asks it, half curious, half teasing: how many gods do you have? Ganesha on the dashboard, Krishna in the calendar, Durga at Navratri, Lakshmi at Diwali, a whole shelf at your grandparents' place.
It's a fair question. And someone asked it once before, out loud, in front of a king. First, a guess.

teach.b: At a great debate in a king's court, a scholar named Shakalya pressed the sage Yajnavalkya: how many gods are there? Three thousand three hundred and six, Yajnavalkya said, giving the old count. Yes, but how many, really?
Three. Two. One and a half.
And finally: one. Which one? The breath of life, he said, which the sages call Brahman.
Each time, the bigger number folds into the smaller, until only one is left. An even older verse says it in five words: ekam sat vipra bahudha vadanti.
Truth is one; the wise call it by many names. That's how a lot of Hindus answer the question.
The many gods are many faces and names of one reality, the way one person can be a mother, a boss and a friend. Not every Hindu puts it the same way.
Some families give their whole devotion to Vishnu, or Shiva, or the Goddess, and see the others within that one. Some honor many, each for a part of life.

teach.h: THE ONE THAT FEELS LIKE YOURS.
teach.b: And almost everyone has an ishta devata: a chosen deity, the form of God that feels like yours. Often it comes from your family; sometimes you find your own. The worry that the others will be upset if you love one most?
Faces of one truth don't compete. So the answer at school can be simple: one truth, many names, and one of them feels like home.

how: Many Hindu homes keep images of several deities; many families have a chosen deity (ishta devata) and a family deity, and devotion ranges from one god held as supreme to many honored together.

games.q: puja was so nice. nani cried a little 🥹 but sam saw her whole shelf after and asked how many gods we have lol. what's the answer??
o: one truth, many names. the gods are faces of one reality, and nani's favorite is her ishta devata, the one that feels like hers.
honestly like millions. we just keep adding them.
just one. the rest are only decorations.
games.why: Yajnavalkya counted the gods down from 3,306 to one, Brahman. Many Hindus see the many gods as faces of one truth, each family with a form that feels like home.

games.q: what's inside the answer — tap the pairs.
p: the form of God that's yours

s: Hindus believe in millions of separate, competing gods
a common Hindu answer is one truth with many names and faces.
an old Hindu verse says truth is one and the wise call it many names
every Hindu explains the many gods the same way
some devote themselves to one god as supreme, some honor many; many see them as faces of one reality.

games.q: your cousin loves Hanuman most and worries the other gods mind. what would many Hindus say?
o: pick one fast, or the others will be upset.
that's your ishta devata. faces of one truth don't compete.
you have to love them all exactly the same.
games.why: many Hindus have a chosen deity, and see it as one face of the same truth.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. Think of the image of God you saw most growing up: on a wall, a dashboard, a shelf. Breathe in.
As you breathe out, say its name once, quietly, as if it were the name of someone who knows you.

wordCard.voice: Ishta devata. Your chosen deity: the form of God that feels like yours. Sixth word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: ishta, chosen or dear, and devata, a deity. the form of God that's yours.

carryVoice: Your line: one truth, many names. Next time someone asks how many gods you have, you've got an answer. Day six.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.9.1–9 (Yajnavalkya and Shakalya: how many gods; the one is breath, called Brahman)
